verdict.headline: The ten-year Treasury yield closed at 5% for the first time since 2007, pushed there by oil
verdict.label: Ten-year reached 5.045% and ended the session at 5.00%, its first close at the level since 2007, after Monday's identical print was rejected. WTI +4.7% to $106.12 and Brent +3% to $108.88 on reported Saudi cargo cancellations with the East-West pipeline still shut. September Empire State fell 13 points to 7.6 with prices paid at 63.1. S&P 500 -0.45% to 7,585.73, Nasdaq -0.78% to 25,981.57, Dow -0.63% to 52,093.11, VIX down to 17.10. Clarity Act cloture failed; BTC -2.9% to $76,834. September 16 hike priced near 91%
verdict.rationale_short:
The ten-year Treasury yield reached 5.045% and ended the New York session at 5.00%, the highest level since 2007 and the first time the figure has survived to a close. Monday's identical print was bought back under the level. The difference between the two sessions was not policy — the committee is in blackout and the quarter-point increase to 3.75%-4.00% was priced near 91% throughout — but oil. WTI rose 4.7% to $106.12 and Brent 3% to $108.88 after reports that Saudi Arabia had cancelled European crude cargoes with its East-West pipeline still shut since September 11. WTI's move being larger than Brent's narrowed the spread on a Gulf supply problem, an unusual direction that points at physical tightness rather than at headline risk: a cancelled cargo is barrels that do not arrive, which is a different fact from a closed pipeline.

The September Empire State manufacturing survey supplied the inflation half of the problem without the growth half. The headline index fell thirteen points to 7.6 while prices paid rose five points to 63.1, above the four-year high set in May, with employment little changed at 10.6 and the average workweek at its highest in nearly five years. Activity decelerating while input costs accelerate is the combination a single policy rate cannot address in one direction, and the long end repriced without waiting for Wednesday.

Equities declined but did not disorder. The S&P 500 fell 0.45% to 7,585.73, the Nasdaq Composite 0.78% to 25,981.57 and the Dow 328.09 points to 52,093.11 — a second consecutive loss, and the third session running in which the equity move is a fraction of the rates move behind it. The VIX fell to 17.10 from 17.29 on the same session, which is a market reducing exposure ahead of a decision rather than hedging against it. Monday's AI-slowdown selling also failed to extend: Qualcomm rose more than 4% to $187.72, AMD 2% and Coherent close to 2%, after Intel fell 7% and AMD 6% the day before on no company statement in either direction.

The day's second resolved event was legislative. The Senate's cloture vote on the Clarity Act failed with more than 40 senators opposed, ending market-structure legislation for 2026 and leaving digital-asset classification to SEC and CFTC enforcement. Bitcoin fell 2.9% to $76,833.83 and ether 3.8% to $2,471.74, while Circle fell about 8% and Coinbase 4.4% — the equities carry the regulatory-clarity premium more directly than the tokens do, and the gap between an 8% decline and a 2.9% one is that difference measured. The arithmetic had been visible for days, which is why the assets fell about as much after the vote as they had approaching it.

The levels that would change the picture: a ten-year back under 4.90% would make today's close a pre-decision hedge rather than a repricing, and a WTI settle under $100 would take the energy input out of the long end with no diplomacy behind it. Neither has happened. Wednesday's information is in the Summary of Economic Projections rather than the rate — Goldman Sachs, having flipped to forecasting this hike, still carries no further increases after September, so a median dot showing two more would mark the widest gap between the committee and the forecasters this cycle.
verdict.lede_short: The ten-year Treasury yield closed at 5.00% after reaching 5.045% — its first close at the level since 2007, one session after the same print was rejected. Oil made the difference: WTI rose 4.7% to $106.12 on reported Saudi cargo cancellations, while the Empire State survey showed activity down thirteen points and input costs at a four-year high. A ten-year back under 4.90% would make it a pre-decision hedge rather than a repricing.

The outcome was arithmetically visible in advance — 60 votes needed against 53 Republican seats — so the decline after the vote was about the size of the decline into it.

trade_setups.thesis: The level was rejected Monday and held Tuesday, with nothing in policy changing between the two sessions — the committee was in blackout and the hike was priced near 91% throughout. What changed was crude, with WTI up 4.7% to $106.12 on reported cargo cancellations, and a regional survey showing activity down thirteen points against prices paid at 63.1. What is forming is a test of whether 5% has become the floor of a term-premium repricing or the ceiling of an energy scare. The counter-evidence is that the VIX fell on the same session, which is not what a market repricing long-run inflation usually looks like.
trade_setups.entry: 5.00% on the ten-year is the level that defines it, with 4.90% below; today's 5.045% high and 5.00% close are the reference prints.
trade_setups.invalidation: A ten-year back under 4.90% in the sessions after Wednesday's projections would say the close was a pre-decision hedge; a sustained hold above 5.00% through a delivered hike would say the long end is pricing an inflation path the rate does not reach.
trade_setups.horizon: Wednesday September 16 through the following week

trade_setups.asset: Crude above $105 and the pass-through lag
trade_setups.thesis: WTI cleared $105 with the Saudi East-West pipeline shut since September 11 and described as out of service for weeks, and reported cargo cancellations now indicate the kingdom cannot route around the outage through Hormuz alone. Refined-product costs reach the CPI basket with a lag of roughly four to six weeks, so this week's barrel lands in the data the committee reads in November rather than the data it reads next month. Against that, energy is already the year's best-performing S&P sector, and a restart announcement is a single headline that removes the premium without any diplomacy behind it.
trade_setups.entry: $100 on WTI below and $110 above are the levels that define it; the September 11 settle of $100.05 and today's $106.12 are the reference prints. The pipeline restart announcement is the observable.
trade_setups.invalidation: A WTI settle back under $100 would say the premium is deflating on its own; a confirmed restart date would do it faster.
trade_setups.horizon: Two to six weeks, through the October CPI reporting period

trade_setups.asset: Digital assets with no legislative path
trade_setups.thesis: The Clarity Act's cloture failure ends market-structure legislation for 2026 and returns digital-asset classification to SEC and CFTC enforcement, which is the status quo the industry spent years and considerable money trying to replace. Bitcoin at $76,834 sits about 3% above the $75,000 area that has held since August. What is forming is a question about whether the bill was a call option the market had already discounted — Polymarket odds of passage in 2026 had fallen to roughly 18% before the vote — or a premium now being removed. The equities answer it faster than the tokens: Circle fell about 8% against bitcoin's 2.9%.
trade_setups.entry: $75,000 on bitcoin is the level that defines it; $76,833.83 is today's reference print, with the exchange and issuer equities the faster-moving read.
trade_setups.invalidation: Holding $75,000 through a week that includes a Fed hike would say the legislative outcome was already discounted; losing it on no fresh news would say regulatory uncertainty is being repriced as a discount.
